Title: Little Women
Author: Louisa May Alcott
full_text_notes: Dialogue heavy.   Has A TON of embedded materials including songs, poems, texts, and letters.   Some of the materials characters are presented as reading. See Chapter 10.
Manual Sample Notes: From Chapter Ten. Sample includes several layers of embedded texts as a character reads aloud a newspaper.

Manual Sample Notes: From Chapter Two. Sample includes several instances of reported thought in which quotation marks are used. Title: Frankenstein
Author: Mary Shelley
full_text_notes: Epistolary, which is used as a frame narrative. The use of frame narrative might make distinguishing narrator and reported speech difficult.
Manual Sample Notes: From "Letter 4" and Chapter 1. Sample includes the transition from the epistolary frame narrative to the embedded manuscript told to the frame narratives narrator by the embedded narrator.

Title: Ruth Hall
Author: Fanny Fern
full_text_notes: Includes instances in which the narrator metafictionally addresses fictional characters: “But, my dear old lady, we beg pardon; we are keeping you too long from that china closet, which you are so anxious to inspect; hoping to find a flaw, either in crockery or cake.”   First chapter contains many scare quotes.
Manual Sample Notes: From Chapters 12 to 15. Sample includes narration in which narrator addresses characters as if they are interlocutors but is actually ironically commenting on them. Selection also includes a fair amount of dialogue and dialect.

Title: Clotel
Author: William Wells Brown
full_text_notes: I’m not sure about this one. It’s a formally interesting text with an interesting publication history.  It contains dialect [though not a ton that involves apostrophe].   It contains epigraphs and  quoted paratextual materials, including slave ads.   It has a few sections with heavily embedded dialogue. See chapter 7.
Manual Sample Notes: From Chapters 2 and 3. Sample includes embedded texts including a song and advertisements. The advertisements do not contain end quote marks in the expected spot.

Title: Our Mutual Friend
Author: Dickens
full_text_notes: Book 2, Chapter 13 is mostly a long speech spoken by a character alone, in which he refers to himself in the third person. Loads of dialogue running across paragraphs.  Last part of the chapter is normal dialogue  Some embedded dialogue
Manual Sample Notes: Froom book 2, Chapter 13 Chapter features a long speech to himself by one of the characters at the beginning of the chapter, with a lot of paragraph length dialogue segment with no closing quote. There is also some embedded dialogue in this part of the chapter. End of the chapter features normal dialogue, but single quotation marks are an added challenge.

Title: Emmeline, The Orphan of the Castle
Author: Charlotte Smith
full_text_notes: This one got a very low score in Muzny et. al’s pipeline, so I think it is worth including just for comparative purposes.  Single straight quotes for dialogue  Several short letters included  Some chapters have epigraphs  Some chapters have footnotes with quotations!
Manual Sample Notes: From Volume 3, Chapter 14 Dialogue is single straight quotes with some contraction and apostrophe. Sample also features a letter written in dialogue formatting, with paragraphs inside the letter that have an opening quotation but no closing quotation. Chapter also includes some French dialogue, the English translations for which are provided in numbered footnotes.

Title: Pamela
Author: Samuel Richardson
full_text_notes: Epistolary  Dialogue reported in the letters is not marked by any typography at all, just ‘said’ tags  Very unclear sometimes when Pamela is speaking via her letters to the reader of said letters, and when she is reporting dialogue
Manual Sample Notes: letter 27 Pamela, the narrator, reports conversations in letters to her parents. Some of the dialogue can be interpreted as direct transcriptions of things other characters said, some are more like summary of what other characters said. The dialogue is never demarked by quotations.

Title: The Wild Irish Girl
Author: Sydney Owenson (Lady Morgan)
full_text_notes: Epistolary Often renders dialogue as speeches (ie, offset/indented) Lots of footnotes, which contain quotes, dialogue etc. Lots of quotes and epigraphs from lit, music etc.  See letters 7 and 8
Manual Sample Notes: Letter 8 Sample includes several quotations from other works, some of which are spoken by characters, and some of which are transcribed by the narrator in his letters.

Title: Unfettered: A Novel
Author: Sutton Griggs
full_text_notes: Heavy use of dialect some of which includes extensive apostrophe.
Manual Sample Notes: Sample includes particularly dense use of apostrophe in quotation.

Title: Lorna Doone
Author: R. D. Blackmore
full_text_notes: Single straight quotes, as well as several passages of dialect rendered using contractions.
Manual Sample Notes: Chose a passage with a decent amount of contraction inside dialogue.
